title: Breath, mind (2.2–2.3)
hook: inside the self made of food, the Taittiriya finds another self, made of breath, and inside that, one made of mind

segments.voice: Yesterday: the five sheaths, and the first of them. Your line was annamaya, the self made of food. Did you look at a meal and see your own body in it? Day three hundred ninety-two, the end of week fifty-six.

A rough experiment, the kind you've already run without meaning to. A person can go weeks without food. Without water, days. Without breath, a few minutes. So which one is holding you together right now? The body you can see is made of lunch. But something is moving through that body every few seconds, quietly, whether you remember it or not. And riding on top of the breath, there's a third thing: the running commentary in your head that is, at this moment, wondering where this is going. The Taittiriya Upanishad noticed all three, and it put them in order. Yesterday it gave you the outer one. Today it goes two layers in.
screen: `WEEKS WITHOUT FOOD. MINUTES WITHOUT BREATH.` → `THE COMMENTARY IN YOUR HEAD.` → `TWO LAYERS IN.`

segments.voice: Chapter two, section two. After the self made of food, the text says: different from this, and inside it, is another self, made of breath. Pranamaya. And it adds a detail people skip. The outer self is filled by this one, and this one too has the shape of a person. So the layers aren't like an onion's skins sitting side by side. They're more like water filling a vessel, taking its shape from the inside. Then the text draws the breath-self like a bird. Prana, the in-breath, is its head. Vyana, the breath that spreads through the body, is one wing. Apana, the down-going breath, is the other. Space is its body, and the earth is its tail, the thing it rests on. And it says why breath matters: prano hi bhutanam ayuh. Breath is the life-span of all beings. Gods, people and animals all breathe after it. Section three goes in again. Inside the breath-self is a self made of mind. Manomaya. And here the bird is drawn out of scripture. The Yajur Veda is its head. The Rig Veda is one wing, the Sama Veda the other. Teaching is its body, and the hymns of the Atharvans are its tail. It's a surprising picture. The mind in this text isn't only a stream of thoughts. It's shaped by the words a person has learned, recited, and carried. One more honest note. The phrase five sheaths, pancha kosha, comes from later teachers. The Upanishad itself just says made of, maya, five times over.
screen: `INSIDE FOOD, A SELF MADE OF BREATH.` · `EACH LAYER FILLS THE ONE OUTSIDE IT.` · `BREATH IS THE LIFE-SPAN OF BEINGS.` · `INSIDE BREATH, A SELF MADE OF MIND.` · then, large: `PRANAMAYA. MANOMAYA.`

segments.voice: Two layers, two minutes. Sit, and start with the body: its weight, the self made of food. Then go one layer in. Feel the breath arrive and leave without steering it. Notice how it fills the body from the inside, belly, ribs, the back of the throat. That's pranamaya. Then go one layer in again. Watch what the mind is doing on top of the breath: a word, a plan, a memory, a tune. Don't chase it. Just notice that it rides on the breath, the way the text draws it. The bell holds the time.
Breath. Prana, the life-span of beings, which in the Taittiriya forms a whole self inside the body, with the self made of mind inside it.

Your line: pranamaya, manomaya. Today, the next time your mind races, check your breath first, and see which one changed. And that's week fifty-six: desire and will, not this, not this, full from full, the teacher's charge, honor your mother, food, and breath. Day three hundred ninety-two.
screen: `WEEK FIFTY-SIX: DESIRE · NETI NETI · FULLNESS · THE CHARGE · MOTHER AS GOD · FOOD · BREATH`

howItsDone: Many Hindus learn the Taittiriya's five layers through Vedanta study and yoga teaching, where breath practice (pranayama) is described as working on the pranamaya layer between body and mind.

match.prompt: the breath-self and the mind-self — tap the pairs.

myth: in the Taittiriya, each inner self fills the one outside it
the outer self is filled by the inner one, and each has the shape of a person.
the Upanishad itself calls them the five koshas
the text says 'made of' (maya). 'five sheaths' comes from later teachers.
the text draws the mind-self out of the Vedas
the Yajur Veda is its head, the Rig and Sama its wings.

fork.setup: you've just learned the self made of food. the Taittiriya says there's another self. where does it say to look?
options: outside the body, in the sky.
inside the food-self: a self made of breath.
nowhere. the body is all there is.
fork.reveal: different from the food-self and inside it is a self made of breath, which fills the outer one and has the shape of a person.

original.note: Sanskrit prāṇamaya: prāṇa, breath, + maya, made of. the second self in Taittiriya 2.2.

trapdoor: what you thought: breath is just air going in and out.
what it means: in the Taittiriya, breath forms a whole self inside the body, with the mind-self inside it.
what a scholar hears: prāṇo hi bhūtānām āyuḥ, breath is the life-span of beings (2.3). the word kosha, sheath, is from later Vedanta, not the Upanishad itself.

sources.ref: Taittiriya Upanishad 2.2–2.3 (the self made of breath; the self made of mind)
Hindu path outline, year two, Block A

notes: Bird-shaped parts given from memory: breath-self (prana head, vyana right wing, apana left wing, akasha body, earth tail); mind-self (Yajus head, Rig right, Saman left, adesha body, Atharvangirasah tail). Please confirm.
The verse 'prano hi bhutanam ayuh' is placed in 2.3 (the verse that opens the section); confirm section numbering, since editions divide anuvakas differently.
Claim that 'pancha kosha' is a later term (e.g. Vedanta manuals) rather than the Upanishad's own: please confirm wording.
Water-in-a-vessel is the script's illustration of 'filled by it' (tenaisha purnah), not the text's image.
